question_html: When a choice must be made between two interpretations of a statutory phrase - one narrower and one wider - what approach does the study material recommend, and how was 'the nature of concern or interest, financial or otherwise' of a director in section 102 of the Companies Act, 2013 interpreted using this approach?

question_html: What does the rule of reasonable construction (also called the Golden Rule) require, and what does the Latin maxim 'ut res magis valeat quam pereat' (also expressed as 'interpretatio fienda est ut res magis valeat quam pereat') mean?

options.A: The rule of reasonable construction requires that the words of a statute be construed so as to lead to a sensible meaning, giving effect to the enactment rather than reducing it to a futility; the maxim means that a construction which gives effect to the statute is preferred over one that would defeat or nullify it - in short, the words of the statute must be interpreted so that the thing (the enactment) may rather have effect than be destroyed
options.B: The Golden Rule requires courts to always adopt whichever construction results in the shortest possible statutory text, regardless of whether it makes sensible practical sense
options.C: The maxim 'ut res magis valeat quam pereat' means 'the letter of the law is supreme and can never be departed from under any circumstances whatsoever'
options.D: The rule of reasonable construction applies only to taxing statutes and has no application to any other category of Central or State legislation

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) The rule of reasonable construction requires that the words of a statute be construed so as to lead to a sensible meaning, giving effect to the enactment rather than reducing it to a futility; the maxim means that a construction which gives effect to the statute is preferred over one that would defeat or nullify it - in short, the words of the statute must be interpreted so that the thing (the enactment) may rather have effect than be destroyed

The Golden Rule (rule of reasonable construction) requires courts to prefer a sensible construction that gives effect to an enactment over one that would reduce it to futility, precisely the sense captured by 'ut res magis valeat quam pereat' - literally, that the thing may rather have effect than perish.

question_html: Under what circumstance does the rule of reasonable construction permit a court to depart from the grammatical/literal meaning of a statute, and how far may that departure go?

options.A: Departure from grammatical meaning is permitted whenever a judge personally disagrees with the policy underlying the statute, with no requirement that the grammatical meaning lead to any absurdity at all
options.B: Departure from grammatical construction is permissible when the grammatical interpretation leads to a manifest absurdity, so that the court may interpret the statute to resolve the inconsistency and make the enactment a consistent whole - but this departure is permissible only to the extent that it avoids the absurdity, and no further, provided the court does not have to resort to conjecture or surmise
options.C: Departure from grammatical meaning is never permitted under any circumstances, since the Golden Rule is, in substance, identical to and interchangeable with strict literal construction with no exceptions
options.D: Departure from grammatical meaning is permitted only when expressly authorised by a specific proviso to that effect, and never on the basis of avoiding an absurd result

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) Departure from grammatical construction is permissible when the grammatical interpretation leads to a manifest absurdity, so that the court may interpret the statute to resolve the inconsistency and make the enactment a consistent whole - but this departure is permissible only to the extent that it avoids the absurdity, and no further, provided the court does not have to resort to conjecture or surmise

The Golden Rule allows departure from grammatical construction only where that construction would produce a manifest absurdity, and even then only to the extent necessary to resolve the absurdity and make the enactment a consistent whole - not as a general license to rewrite the statute or resort to conjecture.

State of UP, where two constructions are reasonably applicable to a statutory provision - one mechanical and grammar-based, the other more vibrant and attuned to the Act's basic intention - which should be preferred, and on what condition does this rule of reasonable construction generally apply?

question_html: When is the rule of harmonious construction applied, and what does the maxim 'generalia specialibus non derogant' mean in the context of resolving a conflict between a general and a specific provision?

options.A: Harmonious construction is applied only when a statute has just one single provision, and 'generalia specialibus non derogant' means that the general rule always overrides any specific exception without exception
options.B: Harmonious construction is applied whenever a court wishes to strike down a statute as unconstitutional, and the maxim relates exclusively to constitutional amendment procedure
options.C: Harmonious construction applies only to conflicts between two entirely different statutes and never to conflicting provisions within the very same statute
options.D: The rule of harmonious construction is applied when there is a conflict between two provisions of a statute, or between the provisions of a statute and the object which the legislature had in view; 'generalia specialibus non derogant' means a specific rule will override a general rule - so where a real conflict cannot be resolved by reading both provisions in harmony, the section that provides for an exception or a specific rule prevails over the section stating the general rule

answer_html:
Correct answer: (D) The rule of harmonious construction is applied when there is a conflict between two provisions of a statute, or between the provisions of a statute and the object which the legislature had in view; 'generalia specialibus non derogant' means a specific rule will override a general rule - so where a real conflict cannot be resolved by reading both provisions in harmony, the section that provides for an exception or a specific rule prevails over the section stating the general rule

Harmonious construction resolves conflicts between two provisions of the same statute (or between a provision and the statute's object) by reading them together consistently wherever possible; where a genuine, irreconcilable conflict exists between a general and a specific provision, 'generalia specialibus non derogant' dictates that the specific rule prevails.

question_html: Under the rule of harmonious construction, how must a statute be read for the purposes of construing any one of its provisions, and what precondition must be satisfied before a court invokes 'generalia specialibus non derogant' to prefer a specific provision over a general one?

options.A: The statute must be read as a whole, and every provision must be construed with reference to the context and other clauses so as to make the statute a consistent enactment rather than reducing it to a futility; the maxim can be invoked only where there is a REAL (not merely apparent) conflict between the provisions - where the words of a statute, on a reasonable construction, admit of only one meaning, that natural meaning prevails and there is no scope to invoke harmonious construction based on equity

options.C: The maxim 'generalia specialibus non derogant' may be invoked even where there is only an apparent, not a real, conflict, so long as doing so produces what the court subjectively considers a more equitable result
options.D: A statute need only be read as a whole when it contains fewer than ten sections; longer statutes are exempt from this requirement under the rule of harmonious construction

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) The statute must be read as a whole, and every provision must be construed with reference to the context and other clauses so as to make the statute a consistent enactment rather than reducing it to a futility; the maxim can be invoked only where there is a REAL (not merely apparent) conflict between the provisions - where the words of a statute, on a reasonable construction, admit of only one meaning, that natural meaning prevails and there is no scope to invoke harmonious construction based on equity

Harmonious construction requires reading the statute as a whole, with every provision construed in light of the others so the enactment remains consistent - and the 'generalia specialibus non derogant' maxim is reserved for REAL conflicts; where a reasonable construction admits of only one natural meaning, that meaning governs without resort to equitable harmonisation.

question_html: What is the effect of the words 'subject to' when used in a statutory provision that covers the same subject matter as another provision, and how does section 13(2) of the Companies Act, 2013 illustrate this?

options.A: A 'subject to' clause always overrides and prevails over the provision to which it refers, the exact opposite of its actual legal effect
options.B: When a provision uses 'subject to' and the same subject matter is also covered by another provision (to which it is subject) and there is a conflict, the latter provision (the one it is 'subject to') prevails over the former - a 'subject to' clause is subservient to the other provision; section 13(2) of the Companies Act, 2013 illustrates this by making any change in a company's name 'subject to the provisions of sub-sections (2) and (3) of section 4', meaning the name change must accord with those provisions of section 4
options.C: The words 'subject to' have no legal effect whatsoever and are treated by courts as mere surplus verbiage to be ignored entirely in construing the provision
options.D: Section 13(2) of the Companies Act, 2013 illustrates a 'notwithstanding' clause, not a 'subject to' clause, since the two terms are used interchangeably in Indian statutes

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) When a provision uses 'subject to' and the same subject matter is also covered by another provision (to which it is subject) and there is a conflict, the latter provision (the one it is 'subject to') prevails over the former - a 'subject to' clause is subservient to the other provision; section 13(2) of the Companies Act, 2013 illustrates this by making any change in a company's name 'subject to the provisions of sub-sections (2) and (3) of section 4', meaning the name change must accord with those provisions of section 4

A 'subject to' clause is subservient to the provision it references, so that in the event of conflict, the referenced provision prevails - as illustrated by section 13(2) of the Companies Act, 2013, under which a company name change must accord with section 4(2) and 4(3).

options.A: A non-obstante clause has exactly the same subservient effect as a 'subject to' clause, and K. Parasurammaiah v. Pakari Lakshman held the two terms to be legally interchangeable
options.B: A non-obstante clause automatically repeals the provisions it references in their entirety, rendering them permanently void for all future purposes, not merely overriding them to the extent of conflict
options.C: A clause beginning with the words 'notwithstanding anything contained' is called a non-obstante clause; unlike a 'subject to' clause (which is subservient to another provision), a non-obstante clause has the effect of making the provision in which it appears PREVAIL over the other provision(s) it references - per K. options.D: A non-obstante clause has no legal effect at all under Indian law and is treated by courts purely as a rhetorical or ceremonial flourish with no bearing on statutory precedence

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) A clause beginning with the words 'notwithstanding anything contained' is called a non-obstante clause; unlike a 'subject to' clause (which is subservient to another provision), a non-obstante clause has the effect of making the provision in which it appears PREVAIL over the other provision(s) it references - per K. Parasurammaiah v. Pakari Lakshman, when this term is used, that clause will prevail over the other provisions mentioned in it

A non-obstante ('notwithstanding') clause reverses the effect of a 'subject to' clause - rather than being subservient, the provision containing it prevails over the provision(s) it references, as held in K. Parasurammaiah v. Pakari Lakshman.

question_html: What does 'ejusdem generis' mean, what is the rule, and what five conditions must be satisfied for the rule to apply?

question_html:
The (hypothetical) Bellview Housing Society Act contains, among others, the following provisions: Section 10 - 'Any transfer of a housing unit shall be subject to the provisions of section 12.' Section 15 - 'Notwithstanding anything contained in this Act, the Managing Committee may sanction emergency repairs up to Rs. 2,00,000 without prior General Body approval.' Section 18 - 'Notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force, decisions of the Society's General Body on internal management matters shall be final.'

Section 15 begins with 'Notwithstanding anything contained in this Act'. What is the scope and effect of this non-obstante clause on the Managing Committee's power to sanction emergency repairs up to Rs. 2,00,000?

options.A: Section 15's non-obstante clause has no legal effect at all and is treated as a subservient 'subject to' clause, requiring the Managing Committee to still obtain prior General Body approval
options.B: Section 15's non-obstante clause automatically overrides every other law in India dealing with housing societies, not merely other provisions of the Bellview Housing Society Act itself
options.C: Section 15 is a non-obstante clause that overrides any other provision CONTAINED IN THIS ACT (the Bellview Housing Society Act) that might otherwise require prior General Body approval for such expenditure - so the Managing Committee's power to sanction emergency repairs up to Rs. 2,00,000 prevails over any conflicting provision within the same Act, though (unlike section 18) it does not, by its own wording, override provisions of any OTHER law
options.D: Section 15's non-obstante clause repeals every other section of the Bellview Housing Society Act in its entirety, leaving only section 15 in force for all purposes

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) Section 15 is a non-obstante clause that overrides any other provision CONTAINED IN THIS ACT (the Bellview Housing Society Act) that might otherwise require prior General Body approval for such expenditure - so the Managing Committee's power to sanction emergency repairs up to Rs. 2,00,000 prevails over any conflicting provision within the same Act, though (unlike section 18) it does not, by its own wording, override provisions of any OTHER law

A non-obstante clause referencing 'this Act' operates at the second of the four illustrated levels - it overrides other provisions of the SAME enactment (the Bellview Housing Society Act) to the extent of any conflict, but section 15's wording does not extend to overriding other, external laws.

Section 2(d) of the Act defines a 'regulated competition' as 'any competition in which prizes are offered for the solution of any puzzle based upon the building up, arrangement, combination or permutation of letters, words or figures.' Sunrise Trivia Ltd. conducts a general-knowledge quiz competition in which participants must correctly answer a series of factual questions arranged in a grid, requiring genuine and substantial knowledge and skill, with success bearing no material relationship to chance.

Applying the mischief rule from Heydon's Case to construe the scope of section 2(d) of the Skill Quiz Regulation Act, what four matters must be discerned?

options.A: (1) What was the law before the Skill Quiz Regulation Act was made; (2) what was the mischief or defect (i.e., disguised-lottery, chance-based exploitation of participants) that the earlier law failed to address; (3) what remedy the Skill Quiz Regulation Act has provided to cure that mischief; and (4) the true reason for that remedy - the court must then construe section 2(d) so as to suppress the mischief and advance the remedy
options.B: The four matters relate solely to Sunrise Trivia Ltd.'s annual revenue, its number of employees, its date of incorporation, and its registered office address
options.C: The four matters are the length of the Act in number of sections, its short title, its date of Presidential assent, and the number of amendments made to it since enactment
options.D: Heydon's Case requires no inquiry into the mischief or prior law at all - only a strict, literal reading of section 2(d)'s wording in total isolation from its legislative history

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) (1) What was the law before the Skill Quiz Regulation Act was made; (2) what was the mischief or defect (i.e., disguised-lottery, chance-based exploitation of participants) that the earlier law failed to address; (3) what remedy the Skill Quiz Regulation Act has provided to cure that mischief; and (4) the true reason for that remedy - the court must then construe section 2(d) so as to suppress the mischief and advance the remedy

Per Heydon's Case, construing section 2(d) requires examining the prior law, the mischief (chance-based exploitation disguised as competitions) that law failed to cure, the remedy the Skill Quiz Regulation Act provides, and the reason for that remedy - then construing the Act to suppress the mischief and advance the remedy.

Applying the mischief rule as illustrated by RMD Chamarbaugwalla v. Union of India, does the Skill Quiz Regulation Act extend to regulate Sunrise Trivia Ltd.'s quiz competition, given that success in that competition depends on genuine and substantial skill and bears no material relationship to chance?

options.A: Yes - the Act automatically and necessarily regulates Sunrise Trivia Ltd.'s quiz simply because it literally falls within the wide dictionary wording of section 2(d), regardless of the Act's declared object or the mischief it was meant to address
options.B: No - consistent with RMD Chamarbaugwalla v. Union of India, where the Supreme Court confined an almost identically-worded definition to competitions in which success does NOT depend on any substantial degree of skill (i.e., gambling-type competitions), the Skill Quiz Regulation Act - having regard to its history and declared object of curbing disguised-lottery exploitation - would similarly be construed as not extending to Sunrise Trivia Ltd.'s genuinely skill-based quiz, notwithstanding the literal breadth of section 2(d)'s wording
options.C: It cannot be determined at all, since the mischief rule has no application whatsoever to any competition or prize-based statute of any kind
options.D: Yes, but only because Sunrise Trivia Ltd. is a private commercial entity rather than a government body, a distinction that the mischief rule treats as decisive regardless of skill or chance

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) No - consistent with RMD Chamarbaugwalla v. Union of India, where the Supreme Court confined an almost identically-worded definition to competitions in which success does NOT depend on any substantial degree of skill (i.e., gambling-type competitions), the Skill Quiz Regulation Act - having regard to its history and declared object of curbing disguised-lottery exploitation - would similarly be construed as not extending to Sunrise Trivia Ltd.'s genuinely skill-based quiz, notwithstanding the literal breadth of section 2(d)'s wording

Section 5 of the (hypothetical) Greenfield Transport Regulation Act provides: 'This Act shall apply to the registration of cars, trucks, motorcycles and other similar vehicles.' A dispute arises as to whether the Act's registration requirement extends to a non-motorized bicycle used for daily commuting.

Applying the rule of ejusdem generis, does the general phrase 'other similar vehicles' in section 5 - following the specific enumeration 'cars, trucks, motorcycles' - extend to cover a non-motorized bicycle?

options.A: Yes - the general words 'other similar vehicles' must always be given the widest conceivable meaning under the rule of ejusdem generis, encompassing every kind of vehicle including a non-motorized bicycle
options.B: Yes - because 'cars, trucks, motorcycles' is a general (not specific) enumeration, ejusdem generis does not apply at all, and 'other similar vehicles' must therefore be read without any limitation whatsoever
options.C: It cannot be determined, since the rule of ejusdem generis applies only to criminal statutes and has no application to a transport registration Act of this kind
options.D: No - since 'cars, trucks, motorcycles' constitute a class or category of MOTORIZED vehicles, the general words 'other similar vehicles' that follow are construed as limited to vehicles of that same kind (i.e., other motorized vehicles), so a non-motorized bicycle - being outside that genus - is not covered by the general words

answer_html:
Correct answer: (D) No - since 'cars, trucks, motorcycles' constitute a class or category of MOTORIZED vehicles, the general words 'other similar vehicles' that follow are construed as limited to vehicles of that same kind (i.e., other motorized vehicles), so a non-motorized bicycle - being outside that genus - is not covered by the general words

Ejusdem generis restricts 'other similar vehicles' to vehicles of the same kind as the preceding specific enumeration - here, all motorized (cars, trucks, motorcycles) - so a non-motorized bicycle, being of a different genus, falls outside the general words.

options.C: Under noscitur a sociis, 'profession' takes its colour from the associated words 'business' and 'trade', restricting 'profession' to activities carried on in a manner analogous to a business or trade (i.e., with some degree of commercial scale or organisation) - as in Dr. Devendra M. options.D: Noscitur a sociis has no application to the word 'profession' at all, since the doctrine is confined exclusively to the interpretation of taxing and revenue statutes
